A '''depression rating scale''' is a [[psychometrics|psychometric]] instrument (tool), usually a [[questionnaire]] whose wording has been [[test validity|validated]] with [[evidence-based practice|experimental evidence]], having descriptive words and phrases that indicate the severity of [[Major depressive disorder|depression]] for a time period.<ref name="pmid12358212">{{cite journal |vauthors=Sharp LK, Lipsky MS |title=Screening for depression across the lifespan: a review of measures for use in primary care settings |journal=American Family Physician |volume=66 |issue=6 |pages=1001–8 |date=September 2002 |pmid=12358212}}</ref> When used, an observer may make judgements and rate a person at a specified scale level with respect to identified characteristics. Rather than being used to diagnose depression, a depression rating scale may be used to assign a score to a person's behaviour where that score may be used to determine whether that person should be evaluated more thoroughly for a [[Mood disorder|depressive disorder]] diagnosis.<ref name="pmid12358212"/> Several [[rating scale]]s are used for this purpose.<ref name="pmid12358212"/>

==Scales completed by clinicians, researchers, and workers ==
Some depression rating scales are completed by clinicians or researchers. The [[Hamilton Depression Rating Scale]] includes twenty-one questions, each having three to five possible responses that reflect increasing or decreasing severity. The clinician must choose the possible responses to each question by interviewing the patient and by observing the patient's symptoms. Designed by psychiatrist [[Max Hamilton]] in 1960, the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale is one of the two most commonly used among those completed by clinicians and researchers in assessing the effects of drug therapy.<ref name=Demytt03>{{cite journal |vauthors=Demyttenaere K, De Fruyt J |year=2003|title=Getting what you ask for: on the selectivity of depression rating scales |journal=Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics |volume=72|pages=61–70|pmid=12601223 |doi=10.1159/000068690 |issue=2|s2cid=29899038 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Hamilton M |title=A Rating Scale for Depression |author-link=Max Hamilton |year=1960 |journal=Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry |volume=23|pages=56–62|pmid=14399272 |doi=10.1136/jnnp.23.1.56 |pmc=495331 |issue=1}}</ref> Alternatively, the [[Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale]] (MADRS) features ten items to be completed for the purpose of assessing the effects of drug therapy,<ref name="Demytt03"/><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Montgomery SA, Asberg M |date=April 1979 |title=A new depression scale designed to be sensitive to change |journal=British Journal of Psychiatry |volume=134|pages=382–9 |pmid=444788 |doi=10.1192/bjp.134.4.382 |issue=4|s2cid=22246215 }}</ref> Another scale is the [[Raskin Depression Rating Scale]] rating the severity of the patients' symptoms in three areas: verbal reports, behavior, and secondary symptoms of depression.<ref name="pmid5768895">{{cite journal |vauthors=Raskin A, Schulterbrandt J, Reatig N, McKeon JJ |title=Replication of factors of psychopathology in interview, ward behavior and self-report ratings of hospitalized depressives |journal=J. Nerv. Ment. Dis. |volume=148 |issue=1 |pages=87–98 |date=January 1969 |pmid=5768895 |doi=10.1097/00005053-196901000-00010|s2cid=39730272 }}</ref> Finally, the [[Occupational Depression Inventory]]<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Bianchi | first1=Renzo | last2=Schonfeld | first2=Irvin Sam | title=The Occupational Depression Inventory: A new tool for clinicians and epidemiologists | journal=Journal of Psychosomatic Research | date=2020 | volume=138 | article-number=110249 | doi=10.1016/j.jpsychores.2020.110249 | pmid=32977198 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Schonfeld | first1=Irvin Sam | last2=Bianchi | first2=Renzo | title=Distress in the workplace: Characterizing the relationship of burnout measures to the Occupational Depression Inventory | journal=International Journal of Stress Management | date=2022 | volume=29 | issue=3 | pages=253–259 | doi=10.1037/str0000261 }}</ref> specifically focuses on depressive symptoms that people attribute to their jobs.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Bianchi | first1=Renzo | last2=Verkuilen | first2=Jay | last3=Sowden | first3=James F. | last4=Schonfeld | first4=Irvin Sam | title=Towards a new approach to job-related distress: A three-sample study of the Occupational Depression Inventory | journal=Stress and Health | date=2023 | volume=39 | issue=1 | pages=137–153 | doi=10.1002/smi.3177 | pmid=35700982 | pmc=10084211 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Schonfeld | first1=Irvin Sam | last2=Bianchi | first2=Renzo | title=From Burnout to Occupational Depression: Recent Developments in Research on Job-Related Distress and Occupational Health | journal=Frontiers in Public Health | date=2021 | volume=9 | article-number=796401 | doi=10.3389/fpubh.2021.796401 | doi-access=free | pmid=34957039 | pmc=8702721 | bibcode=2021FrPH....996401S }}</ref>

==Scales completed by patients==
<div style="background:#CCC;border:1px solid #666;float:right;width:30%;padding:1em;margin:0 0 1em 1em;">
'''The two questions on the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2):'''<ref name="pmid9229283"/>
----
During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?
----
During the past month, have you often been bothered by little interest or pleasure in doing things?
</div>
Some depression rating scales are completed by patients. The [[Beck Depression Inventory]], for example, is a 21-question [[self-report inventory]] that covers symptoms such as irritability, fatigue, weight loss, lack of interest in sex, and feelings of guilt, hopelessness or fear of being punished.<ref name="Beck">{{cite book |author=Beck AT|title=Depression: Causes and treatment| publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press |year=1972 |location=Philadelphia |isbn=978-0-8122-1032-3|page=333}}</ref> The scale is completed by patients to identify the presence and severity of symptoms consistent with the [[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders|DSM-IV]] diagnostic criteria.<ref>{{cite web|title=Beck Depression Inventory &mdash; 2nd Edition|publisher=Nova Southeastern University Center for Center for Psychological Studies|url=http://www.cps.nova.edu/~cpphelp/BDI2.html|access-date=2008-10-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081021161446/http://cps.nova.edu/~cpphelp/BDI2.html|archive-date=2008-10-21}}</ref> The Beck Depression Inventory was originally designed by psychiatrist [[Aaron Temkin Beck|Aaron T. Beck]] in 1961.<ref name="Beck"/>

The [[Geriatric Depression Scale]] (GDS) is another self-administered scale, but in this case it is used for older patients, and for patients with mild to moderate [[dementia]]. Instead of presenting a five-category response set, the GDS questions are answered with a simple "yes" or "no".<ref>{{cite journal |author=Yesavage JA |year=1988 |title=Geriatric Depression Scale |journal=Psychopharmacology Bulletin |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=709–11|pmid=3249773}}</ref><ref name="pmid9720486">{{cite journal |author=Katz IR |title=Diagnosis and treatment of depression in patients with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias |journal=The Journal of Clinical Psychiatry |volume=59 |pages=38–44 |year=1998 |issue=Suppl 9 |pmid=9720486}}</ref> The [[Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale]] is similar to the Geriatric Depression Scale in that the answers are preformatted. In the Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale, there are 20 items: ten positively worded and ten negatively worded. Each question is rated on a scale of 1 through 4 based on four possible answers: "a little of the time", "some of the time", "good part of the time", and "most of the time".<ref name="pmid14221692">{{cite journal |author=Zung WW |title=A self-rating depression scale |journal= Archives of General Psychiatry|volume=12 |pages=63–70 |date=January 1965 |pmid=14221692 |doi=10.1001/archpsyc.1965.01720310065008|hdl=11059/13941 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The [[Patient Health Questionnaire]] (PHQ) sets are self-reported depression rating scales. For example, the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 ([[PHQ-9]]) is a self-reported, 9-question version of the Primary Care Evaluation of Mental Disorders.<ref name="Spitzer99">{{cite journal |vauthors=Spitzer RL, Kroenke K, Williams JB |date=November 1999 |title=Validation and utility of a self-report version of PRIME-MD: The PHQ primary care study. Primary care evaluation of mental disorders. Patient Health Questionnaire |journal=[[Journal of the American Medical Association]] |volume=282 |issue=18 |pages=1737–44 |pmid=10568646 |doi=10.1001/jama.282.18.1737|doi-access= }}</ref> The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) is a shorter version of the PHQ-9 with two screening questions to assess the presence of a [[depressed mood]] and a [[Anhedonia|loss of interest or pleasure in routine activities]]; a positive response to either question indicates further testing is required.<ref name="pmid9229283">{{cite journal |vauthors=Whooley MA, Avins AL, Miranda J, Browner WS |title=Case-Finding Instruments for Depression: Two Questions Are as Good as Many |journal=Journal of General Internal Medicine |volume=12 |issue=7 |pages=439–45 |date=July 1997 |pmid=9229283 |pmc=1497134 |doi=10.1046/j.1525-1497.1997.00076.x}}</ref>

==Scales completed by patients and researchers ==
The '''Prim'''ary Care '''E'''valuation of '''M'''ental '''D'''isorders (PRIME-MD) is completed by the patient and a researcher. This depression rating scale includes a 27-item screening questionnaire and follow-up clinician interview designed to facilitate the diagnosis of common mental disorders in primary care. Its lengthy administration time has limited its clinical usefulness; it has been replaced by the [[Patient Health Questionnaire|Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9)]].<ref name="Spitzer99"/>

==Usefulness==
[[Screening (medicine)|Screening]] programs using rating scales to search for candidates for a more in-depth evaluation have been advocated to improve detection of depression, but there is evidence that they do not improve detection rates, treatment, or outcome.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gilbody S, House AO, Sheldon TA |year=2005 |title=Screening and case finding instruments for depression |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2005 |issue=4 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD002792.pub2 |url=http://www.cochrane.org/reviews/en/ab002792.html |pmid=16235301 |pmc=6769050 |article-number=CD002792 |editor1-last=Gilbody |editor1-first=Simon |archive-date=2009-01-07 |access-date=2008-12-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090107171905/http://www.cochrane.org/reviews/en/ab002792.html }}</ref> There is also evidence that a consensus on the interpretation of rating scales, in particular the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, is largely missing, leading to misdiagnosis of the severity of a patient's depression.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1=Kriston | first1=L.| last2=Von Wolff | first2=A.| title=Not as golden as standards should be: Interpretation of the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression| journal=Journal of Affective Disorders| volume=128| issue=1–2| pages=175–177| year=2011| pmid=20696481| doi=10.1016/j.jad.2010.07.011}}</ref> However, there is evidence that portions of rating scales, such as the [[Somatic symptom disorder|somatic]] section of the PHQ-9, can be useful in predicting outcomes for subgroups of patients like [[coronary heart disease]] patients.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=De Jonge | first1=P. | last2=Mangano | first2=D. | last3=Whooley | first3=M. A. | doi=10.1097/PSY.0b013e31815743ca | title=Differential Association of Cognitive and Somatic Depressive Symptoms with Heart Rate Variability in Patients with Stable Coronary Heart Disease: Findings from the Heart and Soul Study | journal=Psychosomatic Medicine | volume=69 | issue=8 | pages=735–739 | year=2007 | pmid=17942844 | pmc =2776660 }}</ref>

==Mathematical models of the distributions on rating scales for depression==
Because the majority of individuals in the general population have a few or no depressive symptoms, the item score and total score distributions on rating scales for depression are usually skewed to the right.<ref name="Spitzer99"/> Recent research has revealed that item score and total score distributions on such scales exhibit a common mathematical pattern in general population samples.<ref name="t364">{{cite journal | last=Tomitaka | first=Shinichiro | title=Patterns of item score and total score distributions on depression rating scales in the general population: evidence and mechanisms | journal=Heliyon | volume=6 | issue=12 | date=2020 | pmid=33426345 | pmc=7777072 | doi=10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e05862 | article-number=e05862 | doi-access=free | bibcode=2020Heliy...605862T }}</ref> Specifically, total scores on these scales follow an exponential distribution, except for the lower end of the distribution.<ref name="t688">{{cite journal | last1=Melzer | first1=D. | last2=Tom | first2=B. D. M. | last3=Brugha | first3=T. S. | last4=Fryers | first4=T. | last5=Meltzer | first5=H. | title=Common mental disorder symptom counts in populations: are there distinct case groups above epidemiological cut-offs? | journal=Psychological Medicine | volume=32 | issue=7 | date=2002 | issn=0033-2917 | doi=10.1017/S0033291702006049 | pages=1195–1201 | pmid=12420889 | url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0033291702006049/type/journal_article | access-date=2026-01-18| url-access=subscription | hdl=2381/16880 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> Furthermore, responses to all depressive symptom items show a proportional relationship between response options, except for the lower end option.<ref name="w790">{{cite journal | last1=Tomitaka | first1=Shinichiro | last2=Kawasaki | first2=Yohei | last3=Furukawa | first3=Toshiaki | title=A distribution model of the responses to each depressive symptom item in a general population: a cross-sectional study | journal=BMJ Open | volume=5 | issue=9 | date=2015 | issn=2044-6055 | pmid=26369801 | pmc=4577953 | doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008599  | doi-access=free| article-number=e008599 }}</ref> These findings have been confirmed repeatedly by analyzing large-scale data collected from dozens of nationally representative surveys in the US, EU, and Japan.<ref name="k833">{{cite journal | last1=Tomitaka | first1=Shinichiro | last2=Kawasaki | first2=Yohei | last3=Ide | first3=Kazuki | last4=Akutagawa | first4=Maiko | last5=Yamada | first5=Hiroshi | last6=Ono | first6=Yutaka | last7=Furukawa | first7=Toshiaki A. | title=Distributional patterns of item responses and total scores on the PHQ-9 in the general population: data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey | journal=BMC Psychiatry | volume=18 | issue=1 | date=2018 | issn=1471-244X | pmid=29685128 | pmc=5913886 | doi=10.1186/s12888-018-1696-9 | doi-access=free | article-number=108 }}</ref><ref name="a992">{{cite journal | last1=Tomitaka | first1=Shinichiro | last2=Kawasaki | first2=Yohei | last3=Ide | first3=Kazuki | last4=Akutagawa | first4=Maiko | last5=Ono | first5=Yutaka | last6=Furukawa | first6=Toshi A. | title=Responses to depressive symptom items exhibit a common mathematical pattern across the European populations | journal=Scientific Reports | volume=9 | issue=1 | date=2019-10-17 | issn=2045-2322 | doi=10.1038/s41598-019-51499-w  | doi-access=free| article-number=14923 | pmid=31624304 | pmc=6797800 | bibcode=2019NatSR...914923T }}</ref><ref name="q892">{{cite journal | last1=Tomitaka | first1=Shinichiro | last2=Furukawa | first2=Toshiaki A. | title=Mathematical pattern of Kessler psychological distress distribution in the general population of the U.S. and Japan | journal=BMC Psychiatry | volume=21 | issue=1 | date=2021 | issn=1471-244X | pmid=33838666 | pmc=8035733 | doi=10.1186/s12888-021-03198-y | doi-access=free | article-number=188 }}</ref>

==Copyrighted vs. public domain scales==
The Beck Depression Inventory is [[copyright]]ed, a fee must be paid for each copy used, and [[Photocopier|photocopy]]ing it is a violation of copyright. There is no evidence that the BDI-II is more valid or reliable than other depression scales,<ref>Zimmerman
M. Using scales to monitor symptoms and treatment of depression (measurement-based care). In [[UpToDate]], Rose, BD (Ed), UpToDate, Waltham, MA, 2011.</ref> and [[public domain]] scales such as the Major Depression Inventory, the revised Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-R), the Zung Depression scale and [[Patient Health Questionnaire]] – Nine Item (PHQ-9) have been studied as a useful tools.<ref>{{cite journal | pmid=11556941 | volume=16 | issue=9 | title=The PHQ-9: validity of a brief depression severity measure | pmc=1495268 |date=September 2001 |vauthors=Kroenke K, Spitzer RL, Williams JB | journal=Journal of General Internal Medicine | pages=606–13 | doi=10.1046/j.1525-1497.2001.016009606.x}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Terms of Use |website=PHQ Screeners |publisher=[[Pfizer]] |quote=Content found at the PHQ Screeners site is expressly exempted from Pfizer's general copyright restrictions; content found on the PHQ Screeners site is free for download and use as stated within the PHQ Screeners site. |url=http://www.phqscreeners.com/terms |access-date=2 September 2016 |date=2014-09-11 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Screener Overview |website=PHQ Screeners |publisher=[[Pfizer]] |quote=All PHQ, GAD-7 screeners and translations are downloadable from this website and no permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute them. |url=http://www.phqscreeners.com/select-screener |access-date=2 September 2016 |date=2014-12-09 }}</ref>

Other copyrighted scales allow individual clinicians and researchers to make copies for their own use, but require licenses for electronic versions or large-scale redistribution.

==Questions regarding the validity of depression rating scales==
Several research articles have come out in the past several years that investigate the validity of sum-score rating scales for depression.
*{{cite journal |last1=Bianchi |first1=Renzo |last2=Verkuilen |first2=Jay |last3=Toker |first3=Sharon |last4=Schonfeld |first4=Irvin Sam |last5=Gerber |first5=Markus |last6=Brähler |first6=Elmar |last7=Kroenke |first7=Kurt |title=Is the PHQ-9 a unidimensional measure of depression? A 58,272-participant study |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=2022 |volume=34 |issue=6 |pages=595–603 |doi=10.1037/pas0001124 |pmid=35357877 }}
*{{cite journal |last1=Fried |first1=Eiko I. |title=The 52 symptoms of major depression: Lack of content overlap among seven common depression scales |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |date=2017 |volume=208 |pages=191–197 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2016.10.019 |pmid=27792962 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S016503271631312X|url-access=subscription }}
*{{cite journal |last1=Santor |first1=Darcy A. |last2=Gregus |first2=Michelle |last3=Welch |first3=Andrew |title=FOCUS ARTICLE: Eight Decades of Measurement in Depression |journal=Measurement: Interdisciplinary Research & Perspective |date=2006 |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=135–155 |doi=10.1207/s15366359mea0403_1}}
